An examination of average annual new units, focused specifically on the Greenpoint and Williamsburg Neighborhood Tabulation Areas (NTAs), which offers a more granular view than the Council District data depicted above, highlights how dramatically Greenpoint and Williamsburg have outpaced the rest of the City. For example, in the most recent year of available data, 2024, the Greenpoint and Williamsburg NTAs each averaged 1,187 new units, while the other 195 residential NTA’s in the City averaged 175 new units.

Source: New York City Department of City Planning, Housing Database by 2020 NTA (last updated Mar. 16, 2026) (available at ).

As expected, the 2005 rezoning generated enormous increases in housing in Greenpoint and Williamsburg and did so without community opposition. The undeniable truth is that this community has welcomed new housing and undoubtedly will continue to do so. That does not mean, however, that every housing project in this community is appropriate no matter the particulars, and the particulars of this project teach that the housing benefits of the Gotham proposal cannot justify paving the way for enormous towers looming over Bushwick Inlet in violation of the 2005 rezoning compromise.

10. The Commission Should Deny Gotham’s Application to Demap the Museum’s Property as Parkland In Light of the Applicant’s Representations That Demapping Is Not Necessary for the Proposed Project- Also before the Commission is an application from Gotham and the Monitor Museum to demap the museum’s property (Lot 25) as city parkland. See Monitor Point – 56 Quay Demapping (June 12, 2025), C 250326 MMK. The lot was designated as parkland to be included in Bushwick Inlet Park as part of the 2005 rezoning. See City Planning Commission, Calendar No. 6, N 050110(A) ZRK, at 84-85, 123 (Mar. 14. 2005)

(Parcel 19, which was the designation for Lot 25). In approving the rezoning, the Commission expressly addressed the need to balance the designation of the museum’s land as parkland and support for the museum.

In response to testimony regarding the Greenpoint Monitor Museum, the Commission notes that the narrow parcel involved, along the northern edge of the Bushwick Inlet, provides a critical link in the two-mile chain of continuous public access envisioned under the plan. The Commission further notes that the park mapping involves four separate applications, in order to allow for the phased acquisition of parkland. This process permits an opportunity for a dialogue between the City and the Monitor Museum regarding the unique circumstances of this site. The Commission is confident that the proposed park mapping can achieve parkland with continuous public access around the Bushwick Inlet while respecting the integrity of the area’s history.25

Save the Inlet is concerned about the demapping application because it would eliminate Lot 25 from Bushwick Inlet Park. We recognize that Lot 25 is currently privately owned (by the Monitor Museum), but that was the case for all the parcels that the Commission and City Council included in the proposed park in the 2005 rezoning and that the City has since acquired. We also recognize that the Parks Department has disclaimed an intent at this time to seek to acquire Lot 25. But all of this could change should the museum organization ultimately not be able to fund the proposed building and sustained programming, as appears likely. And it would be an egregious mistake to strip Lot 25 of its parkland designation and not have the museum.

In its application, Gotham stated the demapping was intended to remove “an obsolete park designation,” would allow development of a building for the museum, and would “facilitate a mixed use development” of housing. 56 Quay Demapping at 1, 7. At the Community Board, however, the applicant, in response to express questions about the demapping, stated it was unnecessary and that the project as Gotham proposed could proceed unchanged without demapping, which led the committee and full board unanimously to recommend disapproval of the application.26 Though the Brooklyn Borough President recommended approval of the demapping in his report about Gotham’s overall proposal, he barely mentioned the demapping and said nothing to suggest the applicant had changed its position about the demapping having no effect on the proposed project.27

25 New York City Planning Commission, Calendar No. 6, N 50110(A) SRK at 85 (Mar. 14, 2005).

26 Community Board Land Use Committee Report at 5 (Feb. 10, 2026) (available on ZAP) (reporting discussion of need for demapping and 14-0 vote against demapping); Letter to Daniel Garodnick from Dealice Fuller re 56 Quay Demapping Application (reporting 30-0 CB1 vote against application and attaching report from Land Use Committee) (available on ZAP).

27 Brooklyn Borough President, Monitor Point ULURP Recommendation at 4-5, 10 (Mar. 18, 2026) (available on ZAP) (stating obliquely that the Community Board’s reliance on the applicant’s representation about not needing the demapping “raises questions about consistency and clarity between different methods of park designation”).

The applicant has expressly represented as part of the ULURP process that demapping the museum property designated as parkland to be included in Bushwick Inlet Park is not necessary to allow its development to proceed as otherwise proposed. Given this and given the significant public harm that would follow if the land were demapped and the Monitor Museum never materialized, the Commission should deny Gotham’s demapping application

* * *

For all the reasons discussed above, Save the Inlet urges the Commission to adhere to its decisions and commitments in the 2005 rezoning and to reject Gotham’s sweeping applications. Gotham would remain free to proceed with an as-of-right project as allowed under the 2005 rezoning and its agreement with the MTA, a course of action that still would result in relocation of the MTA facility and the creation of new open space while avoiding the threat to the park and inlet posed by Gotham’s high-rise towers. That this might not produce a Monitor Museum building as promised by Gotham does not change the calculus, as Gotham’s plan is impermissible and illusory given the museum’s restrictive deed and precarious condition. As for the prospect of income-restricted housing, that simply cannot outweigh all the problems with the Gotham project, particularly in light of the specifics of Gotham’s claimed housing and the Cityleading contributions Greenpoint and Williamsburg have made to new housing since the 2005 rezoning. Simply put, it would be a grievous error to approve this project on top of Bushwick Inlet.

Respectfully submitted,

Katherine Conkling Thompson Chris Dunn For Save the Inlet

Background 2. The USS Monitor, a warship built for the Union Navy during the Civil War, completed in early 1862, was the first ironclad ( i.e. armored with metal) ship commissioned by the Navy. The Monitor was primarily constructed and assembled by and at Continental Iron Works in Bushwick Inlet, now known as Greenpoint, Brooklyn. The Monitor played a central role in the Battle of Hampton Roads in March 1862, where it fought the CSS Virginia (built on the hull of the scuttled steam frigate USS Merrimack). The battle between these two ships was considered the most definitive naval battle of the Civil War, with the Monitor successfully defending the Union’s fleet of wooden vessels. The battle between these two ironclads marked a turning point in the way naval warfare would be fought in the future.

April 11, 2026 STATEMENT ABOUT SA VE THE INLET PETITION I volunteer with the Save the Inlet, serve as Vice-President of the Friends of Bushwick Inlet Park Inlet Park and the co-chair of Brooklyn Community Board #1’s Land Use Committee, and am a 24-year resident of Greenpoint. As an individual I present to you the voice of thousands of local residents protesting a potentially destructive project planned for development next to the shoreline of Bushwick Inlet and in an already overdeveloped Greenpoint neighborhood. Over the course of the approximately nine months beginning in the summer of last year Save the Inlet, a Greenpoint/Williamsburg born volunteer organization that quickly emerged in response to the existential threat of the Monitor Point proposal, compiled nearly 5,000 signatures from individuals opposing the proposed rezoning of the 40 Quay Street site. I physically created and administered the petition. Core Save the Inlet volunteers relentlessly engaged residents in person in district parks and streets. The petition identified these seven concerns about the Gotham project: 1) Violates the 2005 rezoning agreement which promised this land would serve as a buffer and transition zone—not high-rise towers. 2) Steals parkland by requesting the city to remove park designation from an adjoining property to allow high-rise towers. 3) Ruins Bushwick Inlet just as the surrounding park is being completed (after 20 years!) by turning the park and inlet into luxury amenities for luxury tenants. 4) Luxury housing accelerates displacement, raises rents, and has failed to make communities including ours more affordable. 5) Threatens a rare ecological treasure—Bushwick Inlet is a vital natural habitat in NYC’s harbor and home to diverse wildlife. 6) Adds 1,200 mostly luxury units to an overbuilt neighborhood with many more towers planned and without any infrastructure upgrades to support the increased density. 7) Irresponsible planning that adds thousands of units to a coastal flood zone and devastates resiliency during a climate emergency. The complete sign-on letter with signatories is attached to this statement. Roughly two-thirds of the signatures are from individuals residing in Brooklyn Community District #1.

This petition demonstrates the staggering amount of local human capital dedicated to preserving and protecting Bushwick Inlet, the namesake park and the nearby neighborhood, and to resisting and calling out bad urban planning that would allow for a development that would be so out of place and destructive to its surrounding environment. Therefore, I urge the commission to heed these voices, and recommend No to the Monitor Point land use applications, and adhere to the current zoning designation for 40 Quay Street, that was methodically and thoughtfully plotted out over 20 years ago and holistically included in the aggregate 2005 Greenpoint-Williamsburg Waterfront Rezoning Plan. Sincerely, Steve Chesler Save the Inlet 980 Manhattan Ave. Brooklyn, NY 11222
